title: Kathiyawadi-Inspired Heritage Tomato, Potato & Pea Curry
description: A rich, tomato-led potato curry inspired by Gujarati/Kathiyawadi flavour architecture. A deeply reduced tinned-tomato masala provides the thick, silky sauce, while fresh heritage tomatoes appear twice: some blistered and charred, others barely cooked so they remain juicy and almost fresh.

items.name: Potatoes (Maris Piper or similar), peeled and cut into 3cm chunks
Mixed heritage tomatoes, divided — some for charring, the rest left almost-fresh
Garlic cloves, finely grated or crushed
Green chilli paste, divided across two additions
Soft sun-dried tomato flesh, scraped from the skin and mashed to a paste
Good tomato juice — a controlled cooking liquid kept beside the hob, used only as needed to stop the masala catching, not a set addition
Oil, primarily rapeseed (up to 1 tsp may be swapped for oil from the sun-dried tomatoes)
Halen Môn smoked water, divided across two additions (plus 2-5ml more only if needed after tasting)
Fresh basil leaves, torn or finely shredded
Jaggery or soft brown sugar (optional, to balance acidity)
Small squeeze of lemon or lime (optional, to balance sweetness)

steps.title: Par-cook the potatoes
steps.body: Put the potato chunks into lightly salted cold water. Bring to the boil and simmer for 6-8 minutes. They should be starting to soften around the outside but remain distinctly firm in the centre. Drain thoroughly and leave to steam-dry. Do not fully cook them.

steps.title: Char some of the heritage tomatoes
steps.body: Heat a wide sauté pan, kadai or casserole over fairly high heat. Add a little of the measured oil, then the 125-150g tomatoes. Leave them long enough to develop genuinely dark blistered patches, then turn and char another surface. Remove to a plate. If the pan contains burnt black residue, wipe it out before continuing; browned tomato fond is fine.

steps.title: Make the tarka
steps.body: Reduce the heat to medium and add the remaining oil. Add the mustard seeds, cumin seeds, fenugreek seeds and whole dried chilli. Cook until the mustard begins popping and the cumin becomes fragrant. Let the dried chilli darken slightly, but do not burn it. Add the asafoetida, if using, for a few seconds.

steps.title: Build the aromatic base
steps.body: Add the onion with a small pinch of salt. Cook over medium-low heat for 7-9 minutes, stirring regularly, until very soft and lightly golden. Add the garlic, ginger and ½-¾ tsp green chilli paste. Cook for 2-3 minutes so the first chilli addition loses its raw edge and becomes integrated into the sauce.

steps.title: Bloom the ground spices
steps.body: Lower the heat slightly. Add the ground coriander, turmeric and Kashmiri chilli. Cook for 30-45 seconds, stirring continuously. If the pan looks too dry, add a teaspoon of tomato juice rather than extra oil. Do not allow the spices to scorch.

steps.title: Cook down the tomato masala
steps.body: Crush the tinned whole tomatoes roughly and add them with their juices. Add the sun-dried tomato flesh, thyme sprig, about ½ tsp fine salt and 5ml Halen Môn smoked water. Bring to a lively simmer, then reduce to medium-low. Cook uncovered for 15-20 minutes, stirring increasingly frequently as it thickens. If the masala starts catching before it has properly cooked down, add tomato juice in 20-30ml splashes, allowing each addition to reduce before deciding whether it needs more.

steps.title: Create the silky texture
steps.body: Remove the thyme sprig and whole dried chilli. Using a stick blender, pulse approximately one-third to one-half of the masala. Do not purée the whole pan. Stir the smoother and textured portions together. The sauce should now be thick, glossy and intensely tomatoey; reduce further now if it's still loose. Texture checkpoint: before the potatoes go in, the sauce should already be slightly thicker than the final result you want — the potatoes, peas and late tomatoes will add back a little moisture.

steps.title: Finish the potatoes in the masala
steps.body: Add the par-cooked potatoes and fold them gently through the sauce. If the sauce is too thick for the potatoes to finish cooking without catching, add 25-30ml tomato juice. Cover loosely and simmer gently for 7-10 minutes, stirring carefully two or three times. Once the potatoes are nearly tender, uncover. Crush 2-3 potato pieces against the side of the pan and stir them back into the masala.

timer.label: Simmer the potatoes in the masala

steps.title: Check the consistency
steps.body: Drag a wooden spoon through the bottom of the pan. The channel should stay visible briefly and then slowly close. If the sauce immediately floods back, reduce uncovered before moving on.

steps.title: Add peas and charred tomatoes
steps.body: Gently fold in the peas and the reserved charred tomatoes. Cook for about 2 minutes. The peas should remain bright and sweet and the charred tomatoes should retain some identity.

timer.label: Warm through peas and charred tomatoes

steps.title: Add the second green-chilli layer
steps.body: Stir through ¼ tsp green chilli paste and taste. Do not automatically add more. If your chilli paste is particularly strong, even this may be enough. The intended heat profile is toasted dried chilli, rounded Kashmiri warmth, then a fresher green-chilli lift.

steps.title: Add the almost-fresh heritage tomatoes
steps.body: Very gently fold in the remaining 275-300g heritage tomatoes. Cook uncovered over low heat for only 1½-3 minutes. They should be warmed through, juicy and clearly fresher than the sauce — not cooked down. A few small tomatoes splitting naturally is ideal.

steps.title: Add the late smoke
steps.body: Turn the heat to its lowest setting or remove the pan from the heat. Drizzle over the remaining 10ml Halen Môn smoked water and gently fold it through. Taste after about a minute. If the smoke still disappears beneath the tomato and spices, add another 2-5ml off the heat.

steps.title: Finish
steps.body: Turn off the heat completely. Gently fold through the coriander and basil. Crush a small pinch of Maldon oak-smoked salt between your fingers and scatter it mainly across the surface and the fresh tomatoes. Rest for 2-3 minutes, then taste again. If too acidic, add ¼ tsp jaggery and reassess before adding more. If too sweet or heavy, add a small squeeze of lemon or lime. If under-seasoned, correct ordinary salt first.

notes.label: Design intent
notes.body: Tomato in three forms: a concentrated tinned-tomato base, charred heritage tomato, and almost-fresh heritage tomato. Texture: rich, glossy and spoon-coating, never thin or watery. Heat and smoke: layered for complexity, but restrained enough to preserve the basil, thyme and fresh tomato top notes.

notes.label: Flavour progression
notes.body: Deep tomato and garlic, then mustard, cumin and restrained fenugreek, then soft potato and sweet peas, then rounded red and fresh green chilli, then charred tomato, then a burst of almost-fresh heritage tomato, then coriander and basil, then elusive thyme, then gentle lingering smoke.

notes.label: If it needs adjusting
notes.body: Too acidic: add ¼ tsp jaggery, taste, then consider another ¼ tsp only if needed. Too sweet or heavy: add a small squeeze of lemon or lime. Under-seasoned: correct with ordinary salt first — use smoked salt only for its surface aroma. Smoke too faint: add a few more drops of smoked water off the heat rather than increasing the smoked salt. Heat too restrained: add a very small extra amount of green chilli paste, preferably to individual portions rather than the whole pan.

notes.label: Serving
notes.body: Serve with fresh roti, chapati or paratha, which suit the thick sauce particularly well. For a fuller meal, add a relatively simple dal or plain yoghurt/raita. Avoid pairing it with another elaborate curry — this is intended to be the vegetable centrepiece.

notes.label: Make ahead, storage & reheating
notes.body: For best make-ahead results, cook the masala and potatoes first, then add the peas, charred tomatoes, late green chilli, fresh tomatoes, late smoke and herbs on reheating. Fully finished leftovers keep refrigerated for up to 3 days, though the fresh tomatoes will naturally soften. Reheat only until piping hot — prolonged simmering erases the fresh tomato and herb contrast.

notes.label: Nutrition note
notes.body: Vegetable- and fibre-rich, with peas adding some protein. Not intended as a pulse-heavy one-pot meal — pairing it with dal or yoghurt gives a more complete protein contribution while preserving the curry's tomato-potato identity.
